narrative:
The model has placed you in the category of students at risk of not completing the final year, with a 13 percent probability of failing. That means roughly one in eight students with a similar overall profile ends up failing, and school policy treats this as significant enough to require remedial courses as a safety net.

What is most interesting is that the three strongest factors in your profile actually pointed toward you passing. The single most influential factor was the reason you chose your school: you selected it because it is close to home, a pattern much more common among students who pass than those who struggle. Your clean record of no previous failed classes also worked in your favor, since students who have never failed before generally keep that trajectory. And your clear ambition to pursue higher education after secondary school is the third strongest signal, a goal shared by every single student in the dataset who passed.

So why does the model still flag you? Because a collection of smaller factors, each less influential on their own, combined to tip the balance toward risk. Your weekend alcohol consumption is very high, a pattern seen in barely two percent of passing students. You also lack internet access at home, which is uncommon among successful students. Your family relationships are only fair rather than good, your mother has just a primary education and stays at home, and your free time after school is very low. Together, these paint a picture of an environment that may not fully support sustained academic effort.

The encouraging news is that most of these are within your control. Cutting back on weekend drinking, finding reliable internet access for schoolwork, and talking openly with your family about your goals could meaningfully reduce your risk. With no past failures and a strong desire for higher education already on your side, the remedial courses can help you bridge the gap and finish the year successfully.
